stages.title: Hear up and down
stages.about: Before singing, train your ear to hear whether a note goes up, goes down or stays the same. Both notes are always within one octave, Sa to upper Sa.

chapters.title: Up, down or the same?
chapters.hint: Listen first and answer. The picture appears after you choose. The last two lessons add notes that stay the same.

lessons.title: Big jumps
lessons.theory: The oldest Indian music, Vedic chanting from over 3,000 years ago, was built on hearing up and down: each syllable was sung raised (udatta), lowered (anudatta) or falling (svarita). You are training that same ear. Hum the two notes back before you answer.

lessons.title: Medium jumps
lessons.theory: Bharata's Natya Shastra, written about 2,000 years ago, is the oldest surviving book to name the seven swarams. Musicians then learned entirely by ear, as you are now. If unsure, imagine a staircase: is the second step above or below the first?

lessons.title: Small steps
lessons.theory: The Natya Shastra divides the octave into 22 srutis, steps finer than our swarams, and describes proving them by ear on two identical veenas. Neighbouring swarams like Sa and Ri are much wider apart, so your ear can learn this.

lessons.title: Half steps
lessons.theory: Ga to Ma and Ni to upper Sa are the scale's half steps. Old texts gave the raised Ga and Ni their own names, antara Gandharam and kakali Nishadam, because trained ears noticed even these tiny differences.

lessons.title: All sizes mixed
lessons.theory: Matanga's Brihaddeshi, around the 8th century, is the first known text to define a ragam: a pattern of notes that colours the mind. Every melody is a chain of ups and downs, just like these.

lessons.title: Up, down or same
lessons.theory: Repeated notes have always mattered: Janta Varasa, one of Purandara Dasa's first lessons, is built entirely on them. A note that stays put is a choice, not a mistake.

lessons.title: Small steps or same
lessons.theory: Carnatic music is famous for gamakams, graceful movements around notes, and medieval texts listed ten kinds. Every one depends on the skill you are practising: hearing the tiniest movement, or none.

chapters.title: Sing it up, sing it down
chapters.hint: Now sing. Watch your own line on the graph climb or fall like the reference.

lessons.title: Climb to Pa
lessons.swaras: S , P ,
lessons.theory: Sa and Pa are called prakruti swarams, the natural notes, because they never change in any ragam. That is why the tambura, the drone behind every Carnatic concert, sounds only Sa and Pa.

lessons.title: Fall to Sa
lessons.swaras: P , S ,
lessons.theory: The Sangita Ratnakara describes the voice as coming from three places: the chest for low notes, the throat for middle ones and the head for high ones. Falling to Sa, feel the sound settle lower.

lessons.title: Climb an octave
lessons.swaras: S , S' ,
lessons.theory: The three octaves are called mandra, madhya and tara sthayi. Upper Sa vibrates exactly twice as fast as Sa, which is why the two sound like the same note at different heights.

lessons.title: Fall an octave
lessons.swaras: S' , S ,
lessons.theory: The Vijayanagara empire, whose king Krishnadevaraya was himself a celebrated Telugu poet, was a great patron of music. Purandara Dasa lived and sang in its capital, Hampi.

stages.title: Find your voice
stages.about: One note at a time. No rhythm to keep up with and nothing to memorise.

chapters.title: One note at a time
chapters.hint: Breathe in, then hold each note for four slow beats.

lessons.theory: Sa is Shadjam, 'born of six': ancient texts say it arises from six parts of the body, the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue and teeth. Medieval writers likened it to a peacock's cry.
Ri is Rishabham, likened to the call of a bull. Carnatic music has three varieties of Ri; in Mayamalavagowla, the ragam of these lessons, you sing shuddha Ri, just a half step above Sa.
Ga is Gandharam, likened to the bleat of a goat. Carnatic music has three varieties of Ga, and the one a ragam uses changes its mood: a higher Ga sounds bright, a lower one tender.
Ma is Madhyamam, 'the middle one'. It has two forms, shuddha and prati, and Venkatamakhin split his 72 melakartas exactly in half by them: 36 with each.
Pa is Panchamam, 'the fifth', likened to the song of the koel. With Sa it is one of the two fixed swarams, and the tambura has sounded the pair behind Carnatic singers for centuries.
Da is Dhaivatam, likened to the neigh of a horse. Like Ri and Ga it comes in three varieties, and Venkatamakhin's 72 melakartas use every combination of them with the lower swarams.
Ni is Nishadam, likened to the trumpet of an elephant. It sits just below upper Sa and pulls towards it; the old texts call the raised form kakali Nishadam, the one you are singing now.
Upper Sa completes the seven swarams, the saptaswaras, named in the Natya Shastra some 2,000 years ago. It vibrates exactly twice as fast as Sa, so it is home again, one octave higher.

lessons.title: Sa Pa Sa
lessons.theory: Every lesson begins by tuning to the sruti. An old saying calls sruti the mother of music and laya, rhythm, its father. Sa Pa Sa is the sound of the sruti itself.

lessons.title: Sa Pa upper Sa
lessons.theory: The tambura is usually tuned Pa, upper Sa, upper Sa, lower Sa, so Sa, Pa and upper Sa are exactly what it sounds behind every Carnatic singer.

stages.title: Small steps
stages.about: Move between neighbouring notes. Every phrase starts and ends somewhere you have already been.

chapters.title: Two notes
chapters.hint: Step to the next note, then back.

lessons.swaras: S R
lessons.theory: The first graded lessons were organised by Purandara Dasa (1484-1564). Born Srinivasa Nayaka, a rich merchant, he gave up his wealth to become a wandering singer. He is called the grandfather of Carnatic music.

lessons.swaras: R S
lessons.theory: Purandara Dasa's teaching order is still followed 500 years later: small steps first, then patterns, then songs. Coming down cleanly to Sa is part of every one of them.

lessons.swaras: S R S
lessons.theory: Tradition says Purandara Dasa composed hundreds of thousands of songs in Kannada. Only about a thousand survive, but his teaching method reached every Carnatic classroom.

lessons.swaras: R G R
lessons.theory: For centuries Carnatic music was taught in the gurukula way: the student lived with the teacher's family and learned by repeating short phrases like this one, day after day.

lessons.swaras: G M G
lessons.theory: Ga to Ma is a half step. Venkatamakhin, in his Chaturdandi Prakasika of 1660, worked out every arrangement of steps like these and arrived at exactly 72 parent scales.

lessons.swaras: M P M
lessons.theory: From the 16th century Telugu-speaking Nayaka kings ruled Thanjavur, the heart of Carnatic music. Telugu became the court language, which is a big reason so much Carnatic music is in Telugu.

chapters.title: Three notes
chapters.hint: Climb three notes and come back down.

lessons.swaras: S R G
lessons.theory: Raghunatha Nayaka, a 17th-century Telugu king of Thanjavur, is credited with the modern veena's design of 24 fixed frets. The Saraswati veena on stage today still follows it.

lessons.swaras: G R S
lessons.theory: Ragam Mohanam uses only five swarams: Sa Ri Ga Pa Da. This five-note scale is among the oldest and most widespread in the world, heard in folk music on almost every continent.

lessons.swaras: R G M
lessons.theory: Kshetrayya, a 17th-century composer from Movva near Machilipatnam, wrote Telugu padams sung slowly for dance. Their unhurried phrases are a good model: let every note be heard.

lessons.swaras: M G R
lessons.theory: Tyagaraja's family came from Kakarla in Andhra before settling in Tamil country. Born in 1767, he spent his life in Tiruvaiyaru, composing in his mother tongue, Telugu.

lessons.swaras: G M P
lessons.theory: Tyagaraja is believed to have composed thousands of kritis, of which around 700 survive. Almost all are in Telugu, so as a Telugu speaker you can understand his words directly.

lessons.swaras: P M G
lessons.theory: Every year thousands of musicians gather at Tyagaraja's samadhi in Tiruvaiyaru for the Aradhana and sing his five Pancharatna kritis together. The festival has been held for well over a century.

stages.title: The scale, piece by piece
stages.about: Build the full scale from the lower half and the upper half before joining them.

chapters.title: The lower half
chapters.hint: Keep every note even as the phrase grows.

lessons.swaras: S R G M
lessons.theory: Sa Ri Ga Ma is the purvanga, the first half of the scale. Venkatamakhin's 72 melakartas come from pairing six possible lower halves with six upper halves, then doubling for the two Ma's.

lessons.swaras: M G R S
lessons.theory: Annamacharya (1408-1503) of Tallapaka is the earliest known composer of Telugu sankirtanas. Tradition says he wrote 32,000 songs for Lord Venkateswara, one for every day of his life.

lessons.swaras: S R G M P
lessons.theory: About 13,000 of Annamacharya's songs survive because his family engraved them on copper plates. The plates lay hidden in a vault at Tirumala until they were rediscovered in the 20th century.

lessons.swaras: P M G R S
lessons.theory: Annamacharya's songs, such as 'Brahmam Okkate' and 'Adivo Alladivo', are still sung in Telugu homes and on stage today, more than 500 years after he wrote them.

chapters.title: The upper half
chapters.hint: The same steps, higher up. Reach the upper Sa without pushing.

lessons.swaras: P D
lessons.theory: Pa to Da begins the uttaranga, the upper half. Bhadrachala Ramadasu, a 17th-century tax officer born Kancherla Gopanna, spent royal revenue to build the Rama temple at Bhadrachalam.

lessons.swaras: D N
lessons.theory: Ni is Nishadam, likened to an elephant's trumpet. Ramadasu was jailed in Golconda fort for twelve years for spending that money; the Telugu songs he sang there are still loved across Andhra.

lessons.swaras: N S'
lessons.theory: Muthuswami Dikshitar (1775-1835), one of the Carnatic Trinity, spent years in Varanasi, and his music shows northern influence. He composed mostly in Sanskrit.

lessons.swaras: P D N S'
lessons.theory: Syama Sastri (1762-1827), the third of the Trinity, wrote in Telugu and Sanskrit and loved intricate rhythms. All three Trinity composers were born in the same town, Tiruvarur, within 13 years.

lessons.swaras: S' N D P
lessons.theory: Muthuswami Dikshitar's brother Baluswami is credited with bringing the violin into Carnatic music around 1800. Today the violin accompanies almost every Carnatic concert.

chapters.title: The whole scale
chapters.hint: Join the two halves you already know.

lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S'
lessons.theory: These notes form Mayamalavagowla, melakarta 15. Melakarta names hide their number: in the old katapayadi code 'ma' is 5 and 'ya' is 1, read backwards as 15.

lessons.swaras: S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Purandara Dasa chose Mayamalavagowla for first lessons. Its two halves mirror each other, each with a half step at both ends, which makes the scale balanced and easy to hear.

chapters.title: Small leaps
chapters.hint: Land on the note without sliding up to it.

lessons.swaras: S G
lessons.theory: In 1904 Subbarama Dikshitar published the Sangita Sampradaya Pradarshini, a vast collection of compositions in notation. He wrote it in Telugu, then the language of music scholarship.

lessons.swaras: S P
lessons.theory: Sa to Pa is the ratio 3 to 2, the most consonant leap after the octave. Indian and Greek musicians recognised it independently in ancient times, and nearly every musical culture uses it.

lessons.swaras: S S'
lessons.theory: Sa to upper Sa doubles the pitch. Because the whole system rests on Sa, every Carnatic concert begins with the tambura tuned to the singer's own Sa.

lessons.swaras: S G P
lessons.theory: Sa Ga Pa outlines the major chord. When British bands reached Madras in the 1700s, Muthuswami Dikshitar wrote short Sanskrit songs, called nottuswarams, set to their tunes.

lessons.swaras: P G S
lessons.theory: The Madras Music Academy, founded in 1928, made the December music season famous. Today the season fills Chennai with well over a thousand concerts every year.

stages.title: Your first varasas
stages.about: The first exercises every Carnatic student sings, one line at a time.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 1 and 2
chapters.hint: Lines 2 and 4 of every Sarali are the scale you already know, so learn the new lines on their own first.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali Varasa means 'simple sequence'. Purandara Dasa set these exercises about 500 years ago, and nearly every Carnatic singer since has begun with this one.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R S R S R G M
lessons.theory: Sarali Varasas are in Adi taalam, 'the first taalam', eight beats long and the most used rhythm in Carnatic music. Its full name in the old system is Chaturasra jaati Triputa taalam.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N S' N S' N D P
lessons.theory: Line 3 mirrors line 1. These lessons were passed down orally for centuries; written notation only became common in the late 1800s through printed music books, many of them in Telugu.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S R S R S R G M | S R G M P D N S' | S' N S' N S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: To keep Adi taalam, clap on beat 1 and count 2, 3, 4 on your fingers; then clap and wave for 5 and 6, and again for 7 and 8. Musicians have kept time with these gestures for centuries.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 3 and 4
chapters.hint: Each new line repeats a short group of notes. Count the groups as you sing.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G S R
lessons.theory: Groups of three inside eight beats create a gentle tension. Syama Sastri delighted in cross-rhythms like this; his songs are known as the most rhythmically intricate of the Trinity.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D S' N D S' N
lessons.theory: The Tachur Singaracharyulu brothers of the late 1800s were among the first to publish graded music textbooks in Telugu, putting lessons like this on paper for students everywhere.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 3
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D S' N D S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Before recordings, a student's only reference was the teacher's voice. The first Carnatic gramophone records were made in the early 1900s, and suddenly anyone could hear a master sing.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M S R G M
lessons.theory: Groups of four fit Adi taalam exactly. All India Radio, broadcasting from Madras from 1938, took Carnatic music out of temples and palaces into ordinary homes.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D P S' N D P
lessons.theory: Veena, flute and violin students all begin with these same Varasas; only the instrument changes. Carnatic instrumentalists are taught to make their instruments sing like a voice.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 4
lessons.swaras: S R G M S R G M | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Most Carnatic kritis are in Telugu: Tyagaraja, the best-loved composer of all, wrote nearly every one of his in Telugu. These Varasas are the first step toward singing them.

stages.title: Holding and turning
stages.about: A comma holds the note for one more beat. Phrases now turn back before they finish.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 5 to 9
chapters.hint: Keep the note steady through every comma.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5 - line 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , S R
lessons.theory: The comma for a held beat is how Varasas appear in printed notation books, whether in Telugu, Tamil or Kannada. The same exercises are shared across all of South India.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5 - line 3
lessons.swaras: S' N D P M , S' N
lessons.theory: Holding a note steady against the tambura is called keeping sruti. Many teachers ask students to hold Sa until their voice and the drone seem to merge into one sound.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 5
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M , S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Sarali 5 is the first with a pause inside the line. Long held notes give a Carnatic song its breathing space, and Tyagaraja's slow kritis are full of them.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 6
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D S R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G S' N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: A turn back before the top is a prayogam, a characteristic phrase. Two ragams can share the same notes and still sound different, because their prayogams differ.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 7
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N D | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M G R G | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Turning just below upper Sa is a favourite move. Tyagaraja's 'Endaro Mahanubhavulu', the fifth Pancharatna kriti, salutes all the great musicians who came before him.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 8
lessons.swaras: S R G M P M G R | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M P D N | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Up and back is the shape of a lullaby. The Telugu lullaby 'Jo Achyutananda' is attributed to Annamacharya and is still sung to babies across Andhra.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 9
lessons.swaras: S R G M P M D P | S R G M P D N S' | S' N D P M P G M | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: This zig-zag is a first taste of vakra, or crooked, movement. Some ragams, such as Sri ragam, are built on zig-zag phrases instead of straight scales.

stages.title: Long notes
stages.about: Longer holds and phrases that start from the upper Sa.

chapters.title: Sarali Varasa 10 to 14
chapters.hint: A long note is many beats of the same pitch. Keep it still to the end.

lessons.title: Hold Pa
lessons.theory: Long notes reveal every wobble. The tambura's rich, buzzing tone, which you measure them against, comes from a thread placed under the strings on its bridge, called the jivari.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 10
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , G M | P , , , P , , , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: Long, slow alapanas, where a singer explores a ragam's held notes without words or rhythm, have been the heart of Carnatic concerts for generations. Steady notes like these are their backbone.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 11
lessons.swaras: S' , N D N , D P | D , P M P , P , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: The first Varasa to start from upper Sa. In the early 20th century Ariyakudi Ramanuja Iyengar shaped the concert format still used today, opening with a varnam and building to a main piece.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 12
lessons.swaras: S' S' N D N N D P | D D P M P , P , | G M P D N D P M | G M P G M G R S
lessons.theory: Repeated notes must each be clear. Veena players sound each repeat with a fresh pluck; singers do it with a fresh push of breath, the same skill Janta Varasa will build.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 13
lessons.swaras: S R G R G , G M | P M P , D P D , | M P D P D N D P | M P D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Holds and turns together make a real melody. After the Varasas, Purandara Dasa's next step is the geetham, a simple song; 'Sri Gananatha' is usually the first.

lessons.title: Sarali Varasa 14
lessons.swaras: S R G M P , P , | D D P , M M P , | D N S' , S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: This is the last Sarali Varasa. Traditionally a teacher asked for all fourteen in three speeds before moving on, and finishing them is a milestone every Carnatic student remembers.

stages.title: Twin notes
stages.about: Janta Varasa: every swaram twice, the second with its own fresh stress.

chapters.title: Janta Varasa
chapters.hint: Restart each twin cleanly instead of sliding into it.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 1 - going up
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | P P D D N N S' S'
lessons.theory: Janta is the Telugu word for a pair. Janta Varasas build the control needed for gamakams, the shakes and slides that make Carnatic music sound like nothing else.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D P P | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: M. Balamuralikrishna of Sankaraguptam in East Godavari gave his first full concert at eight and later created new ragams of his own. Even he began with Varasas like this one.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2 - going up
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G R R | S S R R G G M M | R R G G M M G G | R R G G M M P P | G G M M P P M M | G G M M P P D D | M M P P D D P P | M M P P D D N N | P P D D N N D D | P P D D N N S' S'
lessons.theory: Breath control is central to singing: the Sangita Ratnakara lists the qualities of a good singer's voice in detail, steadiness among them. Breathe at the end of each line here.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2 - coming down
lessons.swaras: S' S' N N D D N N | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D P P D D | N N D D P P M M | D D P P M M P P | D D P P M M G G | P P M M G G M M | P P M M G G R R | M M G G R R G G | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: Ghantasala, the legendary Telugu playback singer, trained in Carnatic music at the Maharaja's music college in Vizianagaram before his film career.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G R R | S S R R G G M M | R R G G M M G G | R R G G M M P P | G G M M P P M M | G G M M P P D D | M M P P D D P P | M M P P D D N N | P P D D N N D D | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D N N | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D P P D D | N N D D P P M M | D D P P M M P P | D D P P M M G G | P P M M G G M M | P P M M G G R R | M M G G R R G G | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: The Maharaja's music college in Vizianagaram, founded in 1919, trained many great Telugu musicians. The violinist Dwaram Venkataswamy Naidu was among its famous teachers.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 3
lessons.swaras: S S R R G G M M | R R G G M M P P | G G M M P P D D | M M P P D D N N | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D P P M M | D D P P M M G G | P P M M G G R R | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: Janta practice builds sphuritam, one of the ten classical gamakams, where the second of a pair of notes gets a gentle push from below. Here the pairs climb four at a time.

lessons.title: Janta Varasa 4
lessons.swaras: S S R R S S R R | S S R R G G M M | R R G G R R G G | R R G G M M P P | G G M M G G M M | G G M M P P D D | M M P P M M P P | M M P P D D N N | P P D D P P D D | P P D D N N S' S' | S' S' N N S' S' N N | S' S' N N D D P P | N N D D N N D D | N N D D P P M M | D D P P D D P P | D D P P M M G G | P P M M P P M M | P P M M G G R R | M M G G M M G G | M M G G R R S S
lessons.theory: Purandara Dasa's lessons travelled with the Haridasas, wandering singers who carried devotional songs across South India from the 15th century onward. This Varasa repeats each pair before moving on.

stages.title: Leaping notes
stages.about: Dhatu Varasa: patterns that jump between swarams instead of stepping, so each note must be found fresh.

chapters.title: Dhatu Varasa
chapters.hint: Hear the next note in your head before you jump to it.

lessons.title: Dhatu Varasa 1 - going up
lessons.swaras: S M G M R G S R | R P M P G M R G | G D P D M P G M | M N D N P D M P | P S' N S' D N P D
lessons.theory: In Carnatic terms dhatu is the music of a song and matu its words. A composer who creates both, like Annamacharya or Tyagaraja, is honoured as a vaggeyakara.

lessons.title: Dhatu Varasa 1 - coming down
lessons.swaras: S' P D P N D S' N | N M P M D P N D | D G M G P M D P | P R G R M G P M | M S R S G R M G
lessons.theory: The same leaps from the top. Coming down by leaps tends to fall flat, so aim each landing slightly high in your mind.

lessons.title: Dhatu Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S M G M R G S R | R P M P G M R G | G D P D M P G M | M N D N P D M P | P S' N S' D N P D | S' P D P N D S' N | N M P M D P N D | D G M G P M D P | P R G R M G P M | M S R S G R M G
lessons.theory: The full Dhatu Varasa. Leaping cleanly without sliding is what lets a singer place a gamakam exactly where the ragam wants it.

lessons.title: Dhatu Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S G R M | G P M D | P N D S' | S' , , , | S' D N P | D M P G | M R G S | S , , ,
lessons.theory: Leaps of a third outline a ragam's shape. Ramaswami Dikshitar, father of Muthuswami Dikshitar, is credited with creating ragam Hamsadhwani, which is built on bright leaps like these.

stages.title: Low and high
stages.about: Mandra and Tara Sthayi Varasas: stretch the voice gently below Sa and above upper Sa.

chapters.title: Mandra Sthayi
chapters.hint: Sing low notes gently. Low voice comes from ease, not force.

lessons.title: Mandra Sthayi Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S N. D. P. D. N. S , | S N. D. P. D. N. S , | S R G R S N. D. P. | D. N. S R S , , ,
lessons.theory: Mandra sthayi, the lower octave, is written with a dot below. The Sangita Ratnakara says low notes come from the chest; try this one in Akaram too, singing only 'aa'.

lessons.title: Mandra Sthayi Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S N. D. P. M. P. D. N. | S N. D. P. M. P. D. N. | S N. S R G R S N. | D. P. D. N. S , , ,
lessons.theory: This goes down to the lower Ma. If it is too low for your voice, pick a higher Sa on the Lessons page; Carnatic music lets every singer choose their own Sa.

chapters.title: Tara Sthayi
chapters.hint: Keep high notes light. Stop if your throat tightens.

lessons.title: Tara Sthayi Varasa 1
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S' | S' R' S' R' S' , , , | S' R' G' R' S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: Tara sthayi, the upper octave, is written with a dot above. Teachers traditionally leave it until the voice is settled, because forcing high notes strains an untrained voice.

lessons.title: Tara Sthayi Varasa 2
lessons.swaras: S R G M P D N S' | S' R' G' M' G' R' S' , | S' R' G' R' S' N D P | S' N D P M G R S
lessons.theory: The Sangita Ratnakara places high notes in the head. Range grows slowly with practice, so treat the top note as a visit, not a push.

stages.title: Alankaram
stages.about: Seven patterns, one for each of the seven Suladi taalams, so rhythm and melody are learned together.

chapters.title: Sapta Taala Alankarams
chapters.hint: Clap the taalam while you sing: a clap and finger counts for each laghu, a clap and a wave for each drutam.

lessons.title: Eka Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G M | R G M P | G M P D | M P D N | P D N S' | S' N D P | N D P M | D P M G | P M G R | M G R S
lessons.theory: Eka taalam is a single laghu, four beats in chaturasra jaati, the simplest of the seven. Eka simply means one.

lessons.title: Rupaka Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R S R G M | R G R G M P | G M G M P D | M P M P D N | P D P D N S' | S' N S' N D P | N D N D P M | D P D P M G | P M P M G R | M G M G R S
lessons.theory: Rupaka taalam here is a drutam then a laghu: six beats. Purandara Dasa's first geetham, Sri Gananatha, is set in Rupaka taalam.

lessons.title: Triputa Alankaram - going up
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G M | R G M R G M P | G M P G M P D | M P D M P D N | P D N P D N S'
lessons.theory: Alankaram means ornament. Purandara Dasa set seven Alankarams, one for each of the seven Suladi taalams, so students learn the rhythms by singing them.

lessons.title: Triputa Alankaram - coming down
lessons.swaras: S' N D S' N D P | N D P N D P M | D P M D P M G | P M G P M G R | M G R M G R S
lessons.theory: This one is in Tisra jaati Triputa taalam: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7 beats. Clap on beats 1, 4 and 6. The seven taalams combine with five jaatis, or beat counts, to make 35 taalams.

lessons.title: Triputa Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G S R G M | R G M R G M P | G M P G M P D | M P D M P D N | P D N P D N S' | S' N D S' N D P | N D P N D P M | D P M D P M G | P M G P M G R | M G R M G R S
lessons.theory: Mridangam players learn these taalams with spoken syllables such as 'ta ka di mi'. This spoken rhythm, called konnakol, can be a concert item in its own right.

lessons.title: Matya Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G R S R S R G M | R G M G R G R G M P | G M P M G M G M P D | M P D P M P M P D N | P D N D P D P D N S' | S' N D N S' N S' N D P | N D P D N D N D P M | D P M P D P D P M G | P M G M P M P M G R | M G R G M G M G R S
lessons.theory: Matya taalam is laghu, drutam, laghu: ten beats here. The seven taalams are called the Suladi Sapta Taalas, after the suladi songs of the Haridasas.

lessons.title: Jhampa Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G S R S , R G M | R G M R G R , G M P | G M P G M G , M P D | M P D M P M , P D N | P D N P D P , D N S' | S' N D S' N S' , N D P | N D P N D N , D P M | D P M D P D , P M G | P M G P M P , M G R | M G R M G M , G R S
lessons.theory: Jhampa taalam in misra jaati is a seven-beat laghu, a one-beat anudrutam and a two-beat drutam. Of the seven taalams, only Jhampa uses the anudrutam.

lessons.title: Dhruva Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R G M G R S R G R S R G M | R G M P M G R G M G R G M P | G M P D P M G M P M G M P D | M P D N D P M P D P M P D N | P D N S' N D P D N D P D N S' | S' N D P D N S' N D N S' N D P | N D P M P D N D P D N D P M | D P M G M P D P M P D P M G | P M G R G M P M G M P M G R | M G R S R G M G R G M G R S
lessons.theory: Dhruva taalam is laghu, drutam, laghu, laghu: 14 beats, the longest of the seven. Dhruva means fixed and steady, like the pole star of the same name.

lessons.title: Ata Taalam Alankaram
lessons.swaras: S R , G , S R G M , S R G M | R G , M , R G M P , R G M P | G M , P , G M P D , G M P D | M P , D , M P D N , M P D N | P D , N , P D N S' , P D N S' | S' N , D , S' N D P , S' N D P | N D , P , N D P M , N D P M | D P , M , D P M G , D P M G | P M , G , P M G R , P M G R | M G , R , M G R S , M G R S
lessons.theory: Ata taalam is laghu, laghu, drutam, drutam; in khanda jaati that is 5 + 5 + 2 + 2 = 14 beats. Many varnams, the milestone after geethams, are sung in Ata taalam.
